text: So far you've seen two ways to add subtotals to a GROUP BY: ROLLUP, which follows one fixed hierarchy, and CUBE, which gives you every possible combination. GROUPING SETS is the third option — and it's the one where you get to say exactly which subtotals you want, nothing more and nothing less.

Here's the problem GROUPING SETS solves. CUBE on Color and Size gives you four levels, including a Size-alone subtotal across every color. That's sometimes exactly what you want, and sometimes it's one subtotal too many for the report you're actually building.

GROUPING SETS lets you list the combinations directly. This query asks for three things only: the full Color and Size detail rows, a subtotal per Color, and one grand total using empty parentheses. Nothing about Size alone shows up, because we never asked for it. You get the union of exactly what you list.

GROUPING_ID still works exactly the same way here as it did with ROLLUP and CUBE, because under the hood it's measuring the same thing — which columns in this row are real subtotal NULLs versus actual group values. Order by it and your result lands in a clean, predictable sequence.

Here's the detail that ties all three keywords together: ROLLUP and CUBE aren't separate features. They're shorthand that SQL Server expands into a specific list of grouping sets automatically. ROLLUP always expands to the hierarchy. CUBE always expands to the full power set. GROUPING SETS is the one notation flexible enough to write either of those by hand, or any custom list in between.
Now that you've got all three subtotal tools — ROLLUP, CUBE, and GROUPING SETS — let's put everything from this chapter together. Next up: building a real summary report from scratch.
